The Buccaneer anchovy Encrasicholina punctifer is a small, short-lived engraulid that supports major fisheries in the tropical Indo-Pacific. Anchovies in this genus typically exhibit fast growth, early maturation, and high reproductive output, traits that render them resilient to moderate fishing pressure. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain a maximum lifespan of approximately 2.5 years [am = approximately 2.5 years] when reared in conditions averaging 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], a relatively brief duration that aligns with the rapid life-history pace common among tropical forage fish. The ultimate total length reaches 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], placing E. punctifer among the medium-sized members of its genus, and this asymptotic size is generally achieved within the first year of life. Because the species inhabits warm, productive waters, its growth trajectory is steep, with most somatic development compressed into a narrow seasonal window that coincides with peak zooplankton abundance. These demographic characteristics are important inputs for the stock assessment models used to guide regional harvest quotas.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a relatively small body size compared to its maximum length. Puberty is attained at 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters] of total length, a threshold that corresponds to roughly half the ultimate length and permits early entry into the spawning population. The wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 2.72 grams [Wwp = 2.72 grams], and this modest mass reflects the considerable energetic investment these fish channel into reproduction rather than prolonged somatic growth. The length-weight relationship used to derive this value follows the standard power function employed for engraulids in the region, with parameters fitted from a large sample of wild-caught individuals. This early maturation strategy is widely interpreted as an adaptation to environments where adult mortality is high and unpredictable, favoring a life history that maximizes the number of spawning opportunities before senescence or predation intervenes. The body length at which the onset of gonadal activity first occurs does not vary substantially across the species' extensive geographic range.

The reproductive biology of E. punctifer is characterized by continuous, batch spawning throughout much of the year, a pattern that allows females to exploit ephemeral pulses of planktonic food. Gravid individuals produce multiple clutches over the course of a spawning season, with each batch containing a considerable number of small, pelagic eggs. The maximum reproductive output recorded for this species corresponds to approximately 31 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 31 eggs per spawning event], with females spawning approximately once per day [F_R_i = spawning approximately once per day] when water temperatures are stable at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]; this daily rate is among the highest documented for engraulids of comparable body size and reflects the strong selection pressure for high fecundity in an environment where egg and larval mortality is extremely high. Older, larger females tend to contribute disproportionately to total egg production because they spawn more frequently and release larger batches than first-time spawners. This pattern of reproductive investment is consistent with the income-breeding strategy typical of small pelagic teleosts, which rely on continuous feeding to fuel gamete production rather than mobilizing stored reserves.

The earliest life stages of E. punctifer are tightly coupled to temperature, which governs both the rate of embryonic development and the timing of the transition to exogenous feeding. At the same stable temperature regime of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], the period from fertilization to hatching lasts approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days], a brief incubation that is characteristic of warm-water engraulids. The wet weight at birth is extremely low, estimated at 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], reflecting the minute size of the yolk-sac larva that emerges upon chorion rupture. This initial mass, derived from an egg diameter of approximately 0.7 millimeters, leaves the prolarva with only a small endogenous yolk reserve that must be exhausted before the onset of first exogenous feeding. The rapid depletion of these stores imposes a critical window during which the larva must develop functional vision and a sufficiently wide mouth gape to capture suitable planktonic prey; failure to initiate feeding within this brief period leads to irreversible starvation.

As the larva progresses through the planktonic phase, it undergoes a pronounced allometric shift during metamorphosis, reorganizing its body plan from a streamlined, soft-rayed form to the more robust, fully scaled juvenile morphology. The maximum wet weight achieved by adults of this species has been recorded at 20.5 grams [Wwi = 20.5 grams], a value consistent with the length-weight allometry derived from extensive fishery sampling across its range. For contrast, smaller-bodied individuals that are just beginning to mature weigh considerably less, underscoring the substantial mass gain that occurs between puberty and the attainment of full adult size. Field studies comparing E. punctifer with its congener Encrasicholina heteroloba reveal that the former tends to reach a slightly larger asymptotic mass, possibly due to differences in the thermal regimes of their respective habitats or in the size spectrum of available prey. The post-settlement juvenile phase is relatively brief, and most individuals join the spawning population within their first year, completing the rapid life cycle that sustains the large biomass typical of equatorial anchovy stocks.
